meta.title: CCA Foundations — adaptive question bank
meta.grounding: Exam Guide v0.1 (official task statements + 12 sample questions), The Architect's Playbook (patterns/anti-patterns), @hooeem article. Practice items are constructed strictly from documented rules.
meta.answer_key_note: answer is the correct option letter; rationale explains why + why the strongest distractor fails

questions.source: practice (1.1 anti-patterns)
questions.stem: An agent intermittently stops before finishing multi-tool tasks. The loop continues only when `response.content[0].type == "tool_use"`. What is the root cause?

options.A: The model is exceeding its max_tokens budget mid-task
options.B: A turn can place a text block before tool_use blocks in the content array, so a working tool-use turn is misread as finished
options.C: The tools are returning errors that halt the loop
options.D: stop_reason is unreliable and should be supplemented with text parsing

questions.rationale: Content order isn't guaranteed; text and tool_use co-occur. Drive the loop off stop_reason (continue on 'tool_use', stop on 'end_turn'), never off content[0]. D is the inverted trap — stop_reason is exactly the reliable signal.

distractor_why.A: max_tokens exhaustion is a real failure mode that truncates a turn mid-output, but here the turn completes fine — the bug is misreading a completed tool-use turn, not running out of budget.
distractor_why.C: a tool returning an error is a genuine loop hazard, but the symptom (stopping early on healthy turns) shows tools aren't erroring — the loop is being driven off the wrong field.
distractor_why.D: this is the inverted trap: stop_reason is the reliable completion signal (continue on 'tool_use', stop on 'end_turn') — text-parsing it is exactly the brittle approach you must avoid.

questions.source: practice (1.1 mechanics)
questions.stem: A single assistant turn returns three tool_use blocks. The developer executes only the first, appends one tool_result, and re-sends. The next call fails. Why?

options.A: Parallel tool calls aren't supported; tools must be serialised across turns
options.B: All tool_use blocks in a turn must be answered with all corresponding tool_result blocks (matched by tool_use_id) in a single following user message
options.C: The model should have returned end_turn first
options.D: tool_choice must be set to 'any' for multiple tools

questions.rationale: Every tool_use in a turn needs its matching tool_result (by tool_use_id) returned together in the next user message. Partial/split results break the loop. A is false — parallel calls are valid and faster.

distractor_why.A: serialising tools across turns would be the move only if the API forbade parallel calls — but it doesn't; parallel tool_use is valid and faster, so this misdiagnoses the cause.
distractor_why.C: end_turn would mean the model was finished, but it emitted three tool_use blocks (clearly not done) — the failure is unmatched tool_results, not a missing stop signal.
distractor_why.D: tool_choice:'any' forces the model to pick some tool on a call; it has nothing to do with returning results for already-emitted tool_use blocks.

questions.source: practice (1.1 anti-patterns)
questions.stem: A team makes 'stop after 10 iterations' the primary mechanism for ending the agentic loop. Why does the exam mark this wrong?

options.A: 10 is too low; 50 is the documented default
options.B: Caps either cut off useful work or run unnecessary iterations; the model signals completion via stop_reason. A cap is a safety backstop, not the primary stop
options.C: Iteration caps cause token overflow
options.D: Caps are fine and this is not an anti-pattern

questions.rationale: The word 'primary' is the trap. stop_reason='end_turn' is the completion signal; caps belong only as a backstop.

distractor_why.A: raising the cap (and there is no documented '50 default') treats a number as the fix — but the anti-pattern is using a cap as the PRIMARY stop at all, not picking the wrong value.
distractor_why.C: caps don't cause token overflow; that's context-window growth — this invents an unrelated failure mechanism.
distractor_why.D: making a cap the primary completion mechanism IS an anti-pattern (it cuts useful work or wastes iterations) — calling it fine ignores that stop_reason='end_turn' is the real completion signal.

questions.source: official sample Q7
questions.stem: A multi-agent research system's reports on broad topics consistently cover only a narrow slice (e.g. 'AI in creative industries' → only visual arts). Coordinator logs show it generated three visual-arts-only subtasks. Where is the root cause?

options.A: The synthesis subagent dropped the other sections
options.B: The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow
options.C: The web-search subagents returned poor results
options.D: The report formatter truncated the output

questions.rationale: Subagents executed their assigned scope correctly. Trace to origin: the coordinator never created subtasks for music/writing/film. Distractors blame correctly-working downstream components.

distractor_why.A: a synthesis subagent dropping sections would be the cause if it had received broad subtasks and lost them — but the logs show only narrow visual-arts subtasks were ever created, so nothing reached synthesis to drop.
distractor_why.C: poor web-search results would explain thin coverage within a topic, but the subagents searched exactly the visual-arts scope they were handed correctly — the narrowing happened upstream at decomposition.
distractor_why.D: a formatter truncating output would clip a complete report's tail; here the report was never broad to begin with — trace to origin, not the last stage.

questions.source: practice (1.2 isolation principle)
questions.stem: A synthesis subagent keeps producing reports missing facts that an earlier search subagent clearly found. The coordinator invoked both correctly. Most likely cause?

options.A: Subagents share memory, so the synthesis agent corrupted the search agent's state
options.B: The coordinator didn't pass the search findings into the synthesis subagent's prompt — subagents don't inherit prior context automatically
options.C: The synthesis model is too small
options.D: The search subagent should have called the synthesis subagent directly

questions.rationale: The single most-misunderstood concept: subagents have isolated context, inherit nothing automatically. Everything needed must be in the prompt. D violates hub-and-spoke (subagents never talk directly).

distractor_why.A: shared memory corruption would be the cause if subagents shared state — but they don't; subagents have isolated context, so one cannot overwrite another's findings.
distractor_why.C: a too-small synthesis model would lower quality generally, not specifically lose facts the search agent found — the loss is a missing hand-off, not model capacity.
distractor_why.D: having the search subagent call synthesis directly violates hub-and-spoke (subagents never talk to each other); all routing goes through the coordinator.

questions.source: practice (1.2 skills)
questions.stem: A coordinator always routes every query through the full pipeline (search → analysis → synthesis → report), even trivial fact lookups, adding latency and cost. Best fix per the exam's philosophy?

options.A: Cache all subagent outputs indefinitely
options.B: Have the coordinator analyse query requirements and dynamically select only the subagents a given query needs
options.C: Merge all subagents into one mega-agent
options.D: Increase the model size for speed

questions.rationale: Coordinators should dynamically select, not always run the full pipeline. C destroys the architecture; A is speculative and unreliable (matches the Q9 'speculative caching' distractor pattern).

distractor_why.A: caching indefinitely helps repeated identical work, but it's speculative and unreliable for varied queries and does nothing about routing trivial lookups through the full pipeline.
distractor_why.C: merging everything into one mega-agent destroys the multi-agent architecture (scope partitioning, isolation) instead of fixing the over-routing.
distractor_why.D: a bigger model speeds each step slightly but still runs the full unnecessary pipeline on trivial queries — it treats a routing problem as a horsepower problem.

questions.source: practice (1.3 + Playbook p.23)
questions.stem: A synthesis agent's report contains claims with no source attribution. The search and document-analysis subagents work correctly. Root cause and fix?

options.A: The synthesis model hallucinated; lower temperature
options.B: Context passing dropped metadata; require subagents to emit structured claim→source mappings (claim/evidence/source/confidence) that synthesis preserves
options.C: Add more sources to the search agent
options.D: Switch to a single agent so attribution isn't lost between agents

questions.rationale: Use structured intermediate representations separating content from metadata (URLs, doc names, pages). The loss happened at the hand-off, not in generation. D throws away the architecture rather than fixing the passing format.

distractor_why.A: lowering temperature reduces variance in generation, but the claims aren't hallucinated — the source metadata was dropped at the hand-off, so this fixes the wrong stage.
distractor_why.C: adding more sources gives the search agent more to find, but attribution is lost in passing between agents, not for lack of sources to cite.
distractor_why.D: collapsing to a single agent sidesteps the hand-off but throws away the multi-agent architecture — the fix is a structured claim->source representation, not abandoning the design.

questions.source: practice (1.3 knowledge)
questions.stem: A coordinator cannot spawn any subagents. Most likely configuration cause?

options.A: Its allowedTools list does not include 'Task'
options.B: fork_session is disabled
options.C: The subagents lack system prompts
options.D: tool_choice is set to 'auto'

questions.rationale: The Task tool is the spawning mechanism; allowedTools must include 'Task' or the coordinator cannot invoke subagents at all.

distractor_why.B: fork_session branches an existing session for divergent exploration; disabling it stops branching, not spawning — a coordinator with the Task tool can still spawn fresh subagents.
distractor_why.C: subagents lacking system prompts would degrade their behaviour once spawned, but it wouldn't prevent the coordinator from spawning them at all.
distractor_why.D: tool_choice:'auto' lets the model decide whether to use a tool; it doesn't remove the Task tool — without 'Task' in allowedTools there's nothing to invoke.

questions.source: practice (Playbook p.26)
questions.stem: A web-search subagent given detailed Step 1/2/3 procedural instructions fails on emerging topics and misses tangential sources. Best coordinator-prompt design?

options.A: Add more granular steps (Step 1–10) to remove ambiguity
options.B: Specify research goals and quality criteria (coverage breadth, recency) and let the subagent determine its own strategy
options.C: Remove the subagent and have the coordinator search directly
options.D: Lower the subagent's temperature to follow steps more rigidly

questions.rationale: Coordinator prompts should specify goals + quality criteria, not procedures, to enable subagent adaptability. Procedural micromanagement causes rigid failure on novel topics.

distractor_why.A: more granular Step 1-10 instructions is the right instinct for a fixed, predictable procedure — but it makes the subagent more rigid and worse on novel/emerging topics, the opposite of what's needed.
distractor_why.C: having the coordinator search directly removes the subagent's parallelism and specialisation — it abandons the architecture instead of fixing the over-prescriptive prompt.
distractor_why.D: lowering temperature makes it follow the brittle steps more rigidly, deepening the failure on tangential sources rather than enabling adaptation.

questions.source: official sample Q1
questions.stem: In 8% of cases a support agent processes refunds without verifying account ownership, occasionally refunding the wrong account. Best fix?

options.A: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order/process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID
options.B: Strengthen the system prompt to always verify the customer first
options.C: Add few-shot examples of correct verification
options.D: Add a routing classifier to detect refund requests

questions.rationale: Financial consequences → deterministic enforcement. B and C are probabilistic (non-zero failure persists). D addresses tool availability/routing, not the ordering requirement — the wrong problem.

distractor_why.B: a stronger system prompt is the cheapest nudge and helps in low-stakes cases, but it stays probabilistic — the 8% wrong-account refunds are exactly the residual failures a prompt can't eliminate for a financial gate.
distractor_why.C: few-shot examples teach the verify-first pattern and raise reliability, but never guarantee it — a single miss still moves money to the wrong account.
distractor_why.D: a routing classifier decides which intent/tool to use; it doesn't enforce that get_customer must run before process_refund — it solves a different problem than ordering.

questions.source: practice (1.4 + Playbook p.11)
questions.stem: An agent escalates a complex case to a human who does NOT have the conversation transcript. What must the handoff contain?

options.A: A link to the raw conversation log
options.B: A self-contained structured summary: customer ID, root cause, refund amount (if any), recommended action
options.C: Only the customer's last message
options.D: The full token-by-token transcript dumped into the ticket

questions.rationale: The human lacks the transcript, so the summary must be self-contained and structured. 'Do not dump raw transcripts.'

distractor_why.A: a link to the raw log assumes the human can open the transcript — but the premise is they cannot; a bare link hands them nothing actionable.
distractor_why.C: only the last message strips away the customer ID, root cause, and recommended action the human needs to act without the transcript.
distractor_why.D: dumping the full token-by-token transcript is the explicit anti-pattern — the human needs a self-contained structured summary, not a raw firehose.

questions.source: practice (1.5 + Playbook p.12)
questions.stem: An agent occasionally processes international transfers without the required compliance checks. Emphatic prompt rules still leave a ~3% failure rate. Correct approach?

options.A: Add stronger ALL-CAPS warnings to the system prompt
options.B: Implement a tool-call interception hook that blocks the action server-side and routes to the required check/escalation — removing model discretion
options.C: Add few-shot examples of compliant transfers
options.D: Lower temperature to 0

questions.rationale: Compliance is a 100%-required rule; a single miss is a legal breach. Hooks give deterministic guarantees; prompts/few-shot/temperature are all probabilistic.

distractor_why.A: ALL-CAPS warnings raise prompt salience but remain probabilistic — for a 100%-required compliance check a single ~3% miss is a legal breach, so prompt emphasis is structurally insufficient.
distractor_why.C: few-shot examples teach the compliant pattern and improve reliability, but can't guarantee zero misses — the model still retains discretion to skip the check.
distractor_why.D: temperature 0 makes output reproducible, not rule-enforced — the model can still deterministically choose to skip the compliance step.

questions.source: practice (1.5 knowledge)
questions.stem: Different MCP tools return timestamps as Unix epochs, ISO 8601, and numeric status codes, confusing the model. Cleanest fix?

options.A: Ask the model in the prompt to handle all formats
options.B: A PostToolUse hook that normalises tool results (e.g. Unix→ISO 8601, codes→human-readable) before the model processes them
options.C: Rewrite every MCP server to agree on one format
options.D: Drop the tools that use non-standard formats

questions.rationale: PostToolUse hooks intercept results after execution/before the model, giving clean consistent data regardless of source. C is heavy/infeasible across third-party servers; A is probabilistic.

distractor_why.A: asking the model in the prompt to handle every format is probabilistic and burns reasoning on parsing — a PostToolUse hook normalises deterministically before the model ever sees the data.
distractor_why.C: rewriting every MCP server to one format is heavy and often infeasible for third-party servers you don't control — normalise at your hook, not at every source.
distractor_why.D: dropping the non-standard tools removes capability to dodge a formatting problem that a normalising hook solves cleanly.

questions.source: official sample Q12
questions.stem: A single-pass review of a 14-file PR is inconsistent, misses bugs, and contradicts itself. Best decomposition?

options.A: Split into focused per-file analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass
options.B: Use a larger context window so all files fit at once
options.C: Only review files over 100 lines
options.D: Run the same single pass three times and majority-vote

questions.rationale: Attention dilution; bigger context doesn't fix it (B). Per-file + integration passes address it. D would suppress intermittently-caught real bugs.

distractor_why.B: a larger context window fits all 14 files at once, but the problem is attention dilution across them — more tokens in context doesn't restore the focus a single pass lost.
distractor_why.C: reviewing only files over 100 lines silently skips small files that can carry real bugs — it shrinks the work, not the dilution.
distractor_why.D: running the same single pass three times and voting suppresses bugs that are only caught intermittently — majority vote can drown out a correct minority detection.

questions.source: practice (1.6 knowledge)
questions.stem: Task: 'add comprehensive tests to a large legacy codebase' with unknown structure and dependencies. Which decomposition strategy fits?

options.A: Fixed sequential pipeline with predetermined steps decided up front
options.B: Dynamic/adaptive decomposition: map structure, identify high-impact areas, build a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
options.C: Read every file sequentially into context, then write all tests
options.D: A single prompt asking for all tests at once

questions.rationale: Open-ended investigation → adaptive decomposition generating subtasks from findings. Fixed pipelines (A) suit predictable multi-aspect work like reviews. C is the context-bloat anti-pattern.

distractor_why.A: a fixed sequential pipeline fits predictable, well-understood multi-aspect work (like a PR review) — but here structure and dependencies are unknown, so predetermined steps will be wrong.
distractor_why.C: reading every file into context first is the context-bloat anti-pattern and dilutes attention before any tests are written.
distractor_why.D: a single prompt for all tests at once gives the model no way to discover structure or adapt — exactly the failure on an unknown legacy codebase.

questions.source: practice (1.7 + Playbook p.16)
questions.stem: A support session resumed 4 hours later confidently tells the customer 'expected resolution: 24h' — but the issue is already resolved. Best fix?

options.A: Resume with full history including all prior tool_result blocks
options.B: Resume with human/assistant turns but programmatically filter out previous tool_result blocks, forcing the agent to re-fetch current data
options.C: Never resume; always start fresh with no context
options.D: Ask the customer to confirm the status

questions.rationale: Stale tool_result blocks cause confident outdated answers. Filter them on resume so the agent re-fetches fresh status; keep the conversational turns. C loses useful context unnecessarily.

distractor_why.A: resuming with full history including all old tool_results reproduces the bug — those stale results are precisely what makes the agent confidently quote outdated info.
distractor_why.C: never resuming throws away the useful conversational context unnecessarily; you only need to drop the stale tool_results, not everything.
distractor_why.D: asking the customer to confirm status offloads the fix to the user instead of making the system re-fetch fresh data — it's a workaround, not a fix.

questions.source: practice (1.7 + Playbook p.19)
questions.stem: You want to compare two refactoring strategies that both build on the same prior codebase analysis, without the two explorations contaminating each other. Best mechanism?

options.A: Run both in one session sequentially
options.B: Use fork_session to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline
options.C: Start two unrelated fresh sessions
options.D: Use --resume on the same session name twice

questions.rationale: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline for divergent approaches. One session (A) mixes context; fresh sessions (C) lose the shared analysis.

distractor_why.A: running both strategies sequentially in one session lets the first exploration's context contaminate the second — defeating the clean A/B comparison.
distractor_why.C: two unrelated fresh sessions lose the shared prior codebase analysis both strategies are supposed to build on.
distractor_why.D: --resume on the same session name twice reuses one mutable session, mixing the two explorations rather than branching them independently.

questions.source: official sample Q8
questions.stem: A web-search subagent times out. How should the failure be conveyed to the coordinator?

options.A: Return structured error context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, suggested alternatives
options.B: Return a generic 'error occurred' status
options.C: Silently return empty results
options.D: Terminate the entire workflow

questions.rationale: Structured error context lets the coordinator route/retry intelligently. Generic statuses (B) hide context; silence (C) corrupts synthesis; terminating all (D) is disproportionate. Note: access failure ≠ valid empty result.

distractor_why.B: a generic 'error occurred' status is better than crashing but hides the failure type, query, and partial results the coordinator needs to retry or route intelligently.
distractor_why.C: silently returning empty results is the worst case — synthesis can't distinguish 'access failed' from 'genuinely nothing found' and reports a false 'no information exists'.
distractor_why.D: terminating the entire workflow on one subagent timeout is disproportionate; the coordinator could have retried or routed around a single transient failure.

questions.source: official sample Q2
questions.stem: An agent picks get_customer for order-status queries. Both get_customer and lookup_order have minimal one-line descriptions. Lowest-effort effective fix?

options.A: Expand each tool's description with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries
options.B: Add a routing classifier layer in front of the tools
options.C: Merge the two tools into one
options.D: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt

questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism — proportionate, high-leverage first fix. B over-engineers; the exam rewards the smallest effective change.

distractor_why.B: a routing-classifier layer in front of the tools can disambiguate, but it over-engineers a problem solvable by better tool-description text — the exam rewards the smallest effective change.
distractor_why.C: merging get_customer and lookup_order into one tool destroys a useful distinction and just relocates the ambiguity inside the merged tool.
distractor_why.D: few-shot examples in the system prompt nudge selection, but the primary selection mechanism is the tool descriptions themselves — fix those first.

questions.source: official sample Q9
questions.stem: A synthesis agent needs frequent verification: 85% simple fact lookups, 15% deep analysis. Routing everything through the coordinator adds 40% latency. Best design?

options.A: Give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups; route the 15% complex cases via the coordinator
options.B: Give the synthesis agent every tool the coordinator has
options.C: Make the coordinator a hard dependency for all verifications
options.D: Pre-cache all possible verifications speculatively

questions.rationale: Least privilege: scope a narrow tool to the common case, escalate the rest. B over-provisions (degrades selection); C is the latency cause; D is speculative/unreliable.

distractor_why.B: giving the synthesis agent every coordinator tool over-provisions it and degrades selection reliability (more tools = worse picks) — the opposite of least privilege.
distractor_why.C: making the coordinator a hard dependency for all verifications is exactly the 40% latency cause described — it routes the common 85% case the long way.
distractor_why.D: pre-caching all possible verifications speculatively is unreliable and wasteful — you can't enumerate every fact a synthesis agent will need to check.

questions.source: practice (Playbook p.15 + D2)
questions.stem: An agent with 18 tools frequently picks the wrong one. The exam's principle?

options.A: More tools always improve capability; keep them all
options.B: Too many tools degrades selection reliability — scope each agent to only the tools its role needs
options.C: Switch to a bigger model
options.D: Force tool_choice:'any' so it always uses a tool

questions.rationale: Least privilege again: trim the tool set per role. A broad custom tool alongside built-ins also causes mis-selection (the agent defaults to Grep).

distractor_why.A: 'more tools always help, keep them all' is the inverted trap — beyond a point, more tools degrade selection reliability and the agent picks wrong more often.
distractor_why.C: a bigger model improves reasoning but doesn't fix an 18-tool selection space; it still mis-picks among too many overlapping options.
distractor_why.D: tool_choice:'any' forces the agent to use some tool every turn, which doesn't help it choose the RIGHT one among 18 — it can still grab the wrong tool.

questions.source: official sample Q4
questions.stem: You want a custom /review command available to every developer automatically on clone/pull. Where do you put it?

options.A: In .claude/commands/ committed to the project repository
options.B: In the user's personal ~/.claude/ directory
options.C: In CLAUDE.md
options.D: In a config mechanism that doesn't exist

questions.rationale: Project .claude/commands/ is version-controlled and auto-shared. Personal dir (B) isn't shared; CLAUDE.md (C) is for context not commands.

distractor_why.B: the user's personal ~/.claude/ directory is for your own machine-wide commands — it isn't committed to the repo, so teammates won't get /review on clone/pull.
distractor_why.C: CLAUDE.md carries persistent context/instructions, not invokable slash commands — putting a command there won't register it as /review.
distractor_why.D: this names a config mechanism that doesn't exist — a distractor designed to be eliminated.

questions.source: official sample Q6
questions.stem: Tests are spread across many directories with mixed conventions; you want the correct conventions auto-applied when those files are touched. Mechanism?

options.A: .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter glob path patterns
options.B: A CLAUDE.md in each test directory
options.C: A skill that must be manually invoked
options.D: A slash command run before each edit

questions.rationale: Glob path-matching in .claude/rules/ applies conditionally across scattered files. CLAUDE.md is directory-bound; skills need manual invocation.

distractor_why.B: a CLAUDE.md per test directory auto-loads only when Claude works in that exact folder — but the tests are scattered across many directories with mixed conventions, so this doesn't scale or apply by file pattern.
distractor_why.C: a skill must be manually invoked (or matched by description) — it won't auto-apply conventions just because a test file is touched.
distractor_why.D: a slash command run before each edit relies on you remembering to run it — Rules with glob patterns apply automatically when matching files are touched.

questions.source: official sample Q5
questions.stem: You must restructure a monolith into microservices touching dozens of files. Best Claude Code approach?

options.A: Enter plan mode to explore and design before making changes
options.B: Start editing files directly and iterate
options.C: Ask for the whole change in one prompt
options.D: Disable all tools and do it manually

questions.rationale: Plan mode suits large-scale/architectural/multi-file work — explore and design before mutating.

distractor_why.B: editing files directly and iterating suits small, well-scoped changes — but a monolith-to-microservices split across dozens of files needs exploration and design first, or you mutate blindly.
distractor_why.C: asking for the whole change in one prompt gives no chance to review the approach before large-scale mutation — high risk on architectural work.
distractor_why.D: disabling tools and doing it by hand discards Claude Code's value entirely — plan mode lets it design the change with you, not abdicate it.

questions.source: official sample Q10
questions.stem: `claude "Analyze this pull request..."` hangs waiting for input inside a CI pipeline. Fix?

options.A: Add the -p/--print flag for non-interactive mode
options.B: Pipe 'yes' into stdin
options.C: Use a feature flag that doesn't exist
options.D: Run it in a TTY emulator

questions.rationale: -p/--print is the documented non-interactive mode. Other options reference non-existent or hacky mechanisms.

distractor_why.B: piping 'yes' into stdin is a hack that answers prompts blindly — the documented fix is the -p/--print non-interactive flag, which is purpose-built for pipelines.
distractor_why.C: this references a feature flag that doesn't exist — a distractor to eliminate.
distractor_why.D: a TTY emulator forces interactivity Claude Code doesn't need in CI; -p/--print is the clean one-shot mode.

questions.source: official sample Q11
questions.stem: Two jobs: a blocking pre-merge check (must be fast) and an overnight technical-debt report. A manager wants the Batch API for both to cut cost. Best response?

options.A: Use Batch only for the overnight reports; keep real-time for the blocking pre-merge check
options.B: Use Batch for both to maximise savings
options.C: Use real-time for both for safety
options.D: Avoid Batch because result ordering is unreliable

questions.rationale: Batch allows up to 24h with no SLA — unsuitable for a blocking check; ideal for overnight reports (50% savings). D is a misconception: custom_id correlates results regardless of order.

distractor_why.B: using Batch for both maximises savings but breaks the blocking pre-merge check — Batch allows up to 24h with no latency SLA, unacceptable for something that must return fast.
distractor_why.C: real-time for both is 'safe' but wastes ~50% on the overnight report, which has no latency requirement and is the ideal Batch candidate.
distractor_why.D: avoiding Batch because ordering is 'unreliable' is a misconception — custom_id correlates each result regardless of return order.

questions.source: practice (D4 knowledge)
questions.stem: Tool-use/JSON-schema enforcement guarantees output that is...

options.A: Both syntactically valid AND semantically correct
options.B: Syntactically schema-valid, but NOT necessarily semantically correct — still needs validation logic
options.C: Always semantically correct if temperature is 0
options.D: Free of hallucinated field values

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement ensures shape/types, not truth. You still need validation/retry loops (e.g. calculated_total vs stated_total) to catch semantic errors.

distractor_why.A: 'both syntactically valid AND semantically correct' overclaims — schema/tool-use enforces shape and types, never the truth of the values.
distractor_why.C: temperature 0 makes output reproducible, not semantically correct — a deterministic wrong total is still wrong.
distractor_why.D: schema enforcement constrains field types/shape but can't prevent a hallucinated value that still fits the schema — you need validation logic.

questions.source: practice (D5 + Playbook p.8)
questions.stem: An extraction pipeline reports 94% aggregate accuracy, so it's shipped. In production one document type fails badly. What was the review-design error?

options.A: Accuracy should have been measured per document type and per field, not just in aggregate, before deploy
options.B: 94% is simply too low a bar
options.C: They should have trusted the model's self-reported confidence
options.D: They needed a larger model

questions.rationale: Aggregate accuracy masks per-segment failures; analyse by document type and field, route low-confidence to human review. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated.

distractor_why.B: '94% is simply too low a bar' reframes the issue as a threshold choice — but the real error is measuring only in aggregate, which hides a per-type failure even at high averages.
distractor_why.C: trusting the model's self-reported confidence is unsafe — LLM confidence is poorly calibrated, so it wouldn't have flagged the failing document type.
distractor_why.D: a larger model might raise accuracy but doesn't fix the evaluation blind spot — you'd still ship on an aggregate number that masks per-type failure.

questions.source: official sample Q3 + D5
questions.stem: A support agent achieves only 55% first-contact resolution: it escalates easy cases and attempts hard ones. Proportionate first fix?

options.A: Add explicit escalation criteria plus few-shot examples of when to escalate
options.B: Route based on the model's self-reported confidence score
options.C: Escalate based on detected customer sentiment
options.D: Add a second model to vote on every case

questions.rationale: Explicit criteria + few-shot is proportionate. Self-reported confidence (B) is poorly calibrated; sentiment (C) ≠ complexity; D over-engineers.

distractor_why.B: routing on the model's self-reported confidence is tempting but unreliable — LLM confidence is poorly calibrated, so it would mis-route the easy/hard split it's failing on.
distractor_why.C: customer sentiment measures mood, not case complexity — an angry customer with a simple issue and a calm one with a hard issue both get mis-handled.
distractor_why.D: adding a second model to vote on every case over-engineers a problem solvable proportionately with explicit escalation criteria + few-shot.

questions.source: practice (D5 + Playbook p.23)
questions.stem: Two trusted sources give conflicting figures for the same metric. Best synthesis behaviour?

options.A: Silently pick the higher number
options.B: Annotate the conflict with both values and their sources rather than choosing arbitrarily; preserve claim-source mappings
options.C: Average them
options.D: Drop the metric entirely

questions.rationale: Preserve provenance and surface conflicts (annotate, don't silently pick/average). Arbitrary selection destroys the audit trail and may be wrong.

distractor_why.A: silently picking the higher number destroys the audit trail and may simply be wrong — the exam wants conflicts surfaced, not arbitrarily resolved.
distractor_why.C: averaging two conflicting trusted figures invents a third number that neither source supports and still hides the disagreement.
distractor_why.D: dropping the metric entirely discards real information to avoid the conflict — annotate both values with sources instead.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10
questions.q: How many questions and how long is the CCA exam, and what happens if you leave a question blank?
choices: 40 Q / 90 min; blanks are skipped
60 Q / 120 min; a blank counts as a FAIL (no penalty for guessing)
100 Q / 180 min; blanks deduct points
60 Q / 60 min; blanks are neutral
questions.why: 60 MCQ in 120 min, rapid fire. No penalty for guessing, but a blank counts as a fail — never leave blanks.

distractor_why.A: 40 Q / 90 min with blanks skipped is a plausible-looking exam shape, but the CCA is 60 Q / 120 min and a blank counts as a fail — these numbers are simply wrong.
distractor_why.C: 100 Q / 180 min with blank penalties misstates both the count and the scoring — there's no point deduction for guessing, only the blank-equals-fail rule.
distractor_why.D: 60 Q is right but 60 min is half the real 120-minute window, and blanks are NOT neutral — a blank counts as a fail.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10
questions.q: What is the recommended bar on the practice exam before sitting the real CCA?
choices: Pass once at 720/1000
Score 900/1000 repeatedly, THEN sit the real exam
Just read the guide
Score 80% once
questions.why: Take the practice exam repeatedly until you score 900/1000, only then sit the real one (one attempt).

distractor_why.A: passing once at 720/1000 sets the bar far too low — the guidance is to hit 900/1000 repeatedly before sitting the single real attempt.
distractor_why.C: just reading the guide skips the practice exam entirely — Andrew's warning is the MC wording makes you doubt what you know, so you must drill it.
distractor_why.D: scoring 80% once is below the 900/1000 (90%) repeatable bar and ignores that you get essentially one real attempt.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10

Context management & reliability
Agentic architectures & orchestration (27%)
Claude Code configuration
questions.why: Agentic architectures & orchestration is the biggest at 27% — loops, multi-agent, sub-agents, task breakdown, session state.

distractor_why.A: prompt engineering & structured output is a real domain (~18%) but not the heaviest — agentic architectures lead at 27%.
distractor_why.B: context management & reliability matters (~15%) but is the lowest-weighted domain, not the highest.
distractor_why.D: Claude Code configuration (~20%) is significant but still below the 27% agentic-architecture weight.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10
questions.q: In the customer-support resolution scenario (Claude Agent SDK + custom MCP tools), what is the 'hidden depth' the exam probes beyond the 80% first-contact-resolution target?
choices: Latency optimization
Human-in-the-loop + detecting bad actors / prompt injection
Cheaper model selection
UI design
questions.why: Beyond resolution rate and escalation, the depth is human-in-the-loop plus detecting bad actors and prompt injection.

distractor_why.A: latency optimization is a real concern but a surface one — the scenario's hidden depth is human-in-the-loop plus detecting bad actors / prompt injection.
distractor_why.C: cheaper model selection is a cost lever, not the probed depth — the exam wants escalation and adversarial-input handling.
distractor_why.D: UI design is out of scope for an Agent SDK + MCP support scenario focused on resolution, escalation, and prompt-injection defense.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10
questions.q: What is the KEY nuance the exam cares about for MCP/tool design?
choices: Server uptime
The difference between a personal MCP server and a TEAM one (permissions + per-role access levels)
Using the fastest transport
Number of tools exposed
questions.why: Team deployments differ fundamentally from personal ones: permissions, per-role access levels, least-privilege scoping.

distractor_why.A: server uptime is an ops concern, not the design nuance the exam probes — that's the personal-vs-team permission/access-level distinction.
distractor_why.C: choosing the fastest transport (stdio vs SSE) is incidental; the key nuance is per-role permissions and least-privilege scoping.
distractor_why.D: raw number of tools exposed isn't the point — it's WHICH tools each role may access (per-role scoping), not the count.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10

choices: Theory you can recite
What you implement and the trade-offs you understand (practitioner)
Memorized API parameter names
The history of Claude models
questions.why: It's a 300-level practitioner exam — it tests implementation + trade-offs, not recitation. 'The bluffing gets exposed.'

distractor_why.A: 'theory you can recite' is exactly what the exam does NOT test — Goda's line is 'the bluffing gets exposed'.
distractor_why.C: memorized API parameter names are recitation, not the implementation-and-trade-offs the 300-level practitioner exam targets.
distractor_why.D: the history of Claude models is trivia — the exam tests what you build and the trade-offs you understand.

questions.source: autonomee_certpath_june10
questions.q: In the 'code generation with Claude Code' scenario, what judgment does the exam expect?
choices: Always biggest model
When to use plan mode vs direct execution (+ custom slash commands)
Disable tools
Avoid refactoring
questions.why: Integrate Claude Code into dev workflows with custom slash commands; choose plan mode vs direct execution.

distractor_why.A: 'always biggest model' is a non-judgment — the scenario expects choosing plan mode vs direct execution and using custom slash commands.
distractor_why.C: disabling tools cripples Claude Code; the scenario is about integrating it into dev workflows, not stripping it.
distractor_why.D: avoiding refactoring contradicts the scenario, which centres on refactoring, debugging, and documentation in real workflows.
